metaDesc: Thai Buffalo Village in Si Prachan, Suphan Buri, Thailand — watch the trained buffalo show, ride and feed buffalo, tour the Thai houses. Great for kids, with show times and hours.

h1:
Thai Buffalo Village
Get Up Close With Buffalo, Kid-Friendly
intro: If you've got kids in the car and want somewhere that's genuinely fun and teaches real Thai country life, the Thai Buffalo Conservation Village in Si Prachan is the answer a lot of families come back to. You get a trained buffalo show, feeding the buffalo up close, riding one out in the field, walking through wooden Thai houses at the edge of the paddies, and seeing old-time farmer life you can actually touch.

blocks.html: The Thai Buffalo Conservation Village — or what locals just call the Suphan Buri buffalo village — has been open since 2002, spread across roughly 70 rai (about 11 hectares) along the Suphan Buri–Chai Nat road in Wang Nam Sap, Si Prachan district. The idea here is simple: preserve a picture of old rural Thai farming life for younger generations to see, from the buffalo that worked the rice paddies, to the wooden Thai houses, the rice-threshing yard, and farming tools that plenty of kids today have never laid eyes on.

What makes this place so good for families is that kids get close to real buffalo, can feed them, and watch them perform in the show ring — plus the grounds are easy to walk, with lots of shade. It's not the kind of place where you trudge so far the kids start whining. A full walk-through takes about 1–2 hours, so it works as a stop along the way or as the main event of a family trip.

items: The trained buffalo show — the star of the place. The buffalo follow the handler's cues: bowing, nodding, "smiling," running under bars, and acting out a whole rice-ploughing story. Kids tend to sit there without blinking.
Riding a buffalo in the field — the kids' favourite. They sit on the back of a real buffalo with a handler leading it, so it's safe and makes for great photos.
Feeding the buffalo — there's grass and vegetables to hand-feed the buffalo in the pen up close. Some of them are softies and walk right over to you.
Thai houses by the paddies — several teak Thai-style houses arranged as a cluster to walk through and photograph, with an old-times feel.
Thai Farmer Museum — a collection of old farming tools: ploughs, ox carts, foot-powered rice mills, and threshing gear, with explanations of the traditional way of working the land.
The "Gin Fae Doo Fai" café — a spot to sip coffee and rest your legs over a view of the rice fields and buffalo. The name is a cute Suphan-style pun (roughly "sip coffee, watch buffalo").

blocks.text: What Time Are the Buffalo Shows?

blocks.html: The buffalo show is the main reason people come, so check the times before you go — turn up at the wrong hour and you could miss it. Here are the regular show slots (they may shift with the season and crowd size; you can call ahead to confirm at 08 1358 7347).

items.name: Weekdays (Mon–Fri)
items.blurb: Two shows on weekdays, morning and afternoon. It's quieter then, easy to watch, and kids get closer to the buffalo — good if you want to skip the crowds.

items.name: Weekends & public holidays
items.blurb: Three shows on holidays, covering morning to afternoon, so you've got a slot to spare even if you arrive late. It's busier, though, so come a little before showtime to grab a front-row seat.

blocks.title: How to Time It Just Right
blocks.html: Aim to arrive about 30–45 minutes before showtime so you can walk around, feed the buffalo, and visit the pen first, then sit down for the show. After it wraps, go for the buffalo ride. Order it this way and the kids don't get bored or feel rushed.

blocks.text: How to Make a Kids' Visit Fun and Safe

items: Wear shoes you don't mind getting dirty — the ground is dirt and paddy field, with natural mud in spots. Sneakers or strap-back sandals are about right.
Bring a hat and water — a lot of the activities are outdoors and the afternoon sun is strong, so pack a hat and drinking water.
Keep little ones close near the buffalo — the buffalo here are tame and handlers look after them, but they're big animals, so hold your child's hand and follow the staff's instructions.
Bring cash — the buffalo ride, buffalo feed, and some food stalls are easier to pay for in cash.

blocks.html: On admission and activity fees, the info varies from source to source. At times there's no main entry charge but activities (like the buffalo ride and feeding) are priced separately; at other times there's an entry fee of around 30–50 THB for Thais. To be sure, it's best to call the village before you go so you can bring enough cash.

blocks.text: A Full Day With the Kids

blocks.label: Morning
blocks.title: Arrive at the buffalo village before the 11am show

items.activity: Arrive and head into the Thai-house zone and the farmer museum so the kids can see the ploughs, ox carts, and farming gear.
Go to the buffalo pen, buy grass/veg to feed them, and get to know the buffalo before the show.
Head into the ring for the day's first trained buffalo show.
items.note: Grab a front-row seat before it starts

blocks.label: Midday–Afternoon
blocks.title: Ride a buffalo, break for lunch, then get your photos

items.activity: Break for lunch at the "Gin Fae Doo Fai" café — sip coffee over the rice-field view.
Queue up for the buffalo ride in the field, with a handler leading it, and get photos on the buffalo's back.
Walk around for photos of the Thai houses, then pick up veg and fruit from the local stalls at the entrance before heading off.
items.note: Stalls out front sell at local prices

blocks.html: If you want to keep going into the afternoon, it's about a 20–25 minute drive from Si Prachan into Suphan Buri town, where you can easily fit in the Banharn-Jaemsai Tower or the Dragon Descendants Museum in the same day.

The village sits along the Suphan Buri–Chai Nat road (Highway 340) in the Si Prachan district, about a 20-minute drive north of Suphan Buri town. The sign is easy to spot roadside, and there's a large parking lot in the grounds — driving yourself is the most convenient option. Coming from Bangkok, it's roughly 1.5 to 2 hours. Open daily, 09:00–18:00.

faq.q: What time does the Thai Buffalo Village open?
faq.a: Open daily with no closing days, 09:00–18:00. It's on the Suphan Buri–Chai Nat road in Wang Nam Sap, Si Prachan district, Suphan Buri province.

faq.q: What time are the buffalo shows?
faq.a: Monday–Friday there are 2 shows, at 11:00 and 13:00. On Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays there are 3 shows, at 11:00, 13:30, and 15:00. Call ahead at 08 1358 7347 before you go, as the times can change.

Admission info varies between sources. At times there's no main entry charge but activities are priced separately, such as the buffalo ride and feeding; at other times there's an entry fee of around 30–50 THB for Thais. We'd suggest bringing cash and calling ahead before you go.

faq.q: Is it suitable for young children?
faq.a: Very much so. Kids get to feed the buffalo, ride one, and watch the show up close, and the grounds are easy to walk with lots of shade — a full walk-through takes about 1–2 hours. Just keep an eye on little ones near the buffalo and follow the staff's instructions.

faq.q: How long does a visit take?
faq.a: Walking around and catching one show takes about 1–2 hours. If you also want to ride a buffalo, feed them, and sit at the café, allow around half a day.
